sections.title: Population level
sections.headline: 2025 Year-end: 7,508.7 thousand
sections.insight: Year-end population moved from 3,195.3 thousand in 1961 Year-end to 7,508.7 thousand in 2025 Year-end. The historical peak was 7,527.9 thousand in 2023 Year-end.
sections.chart_note: Year-end population, both sexes, all ages. Event lines mark major external shocks where they fall within the time range.

support_charts.title: Decade change
support_charts.subtext: Absolute change versus the prior decade anchor.

support_charts.title: Recent slope
support_charts.subtext: The last 14 annual observations, isolated from the long history.

sections.commentary: The long history still trends upward, but the late-series slope is flatter than in the earlier expansion decades.

sources.title: Population by sex and age group

sections.title: Population growth components
sections.headline: 2025 Year-end: growth 8.1 thousand, net movement 27.1 thousand
sections.insight: Population growth peaked at 254.8 thousand in 1979 Year-end. In the latest year, births were 31.1 thousand and deaths were 50.0 thousand.
sections.chart_note: Annual year-end population growth history. Event lines provide timing context for shocks and recoveries.

support_charts.title: Natural increase
support_charts.subtext: Births minus deaths across the full series.

support_charts.title: Latest drivers
support_charts.subtext: Latest year comparison across the main growth drivers.

sections.commentary: Natural increase has weakened over time, so swings in net movement now have a much larger influence on the headline growth result.

sections.title: Ageing and dependency
sections.headline: 2026: median age 49.8, dependency ratio 543.0
sections.insight: Median age rose by 23.1 years over the series, while the total dependency ratio increased from 455.0 to 543.0.
sections.chart_note: Annual population ageing indicators, excluding foreign domestic helpers. Event lines matter less here because the shift is structural rather than cyclical.

support_charts.title: Dependency ratio
support_charts.subtext: How many dependants are supported per 1,000 working-age people.

support_charts.title: Median age milestones
support_charts.subtext: Start, latest and peak age markers from the full history.

sections.commentary: The ageing story is persistent across shocks: short crises interrupt economic series, but they do not reverse the demographic direction of travel.

sources.title: Dependency ratio and median age of population

sections.title: Fertility pressure
sections.headline: 2025: TFR 733.00, crude birth rate 4.1 per 1,000
sections.insight: Total fertility fell from a peak of 3,459.00 in 1971 to 733.00 in the latest release.
sections.chart_note: Annual fertility indicators. Event lines are included for orientation, but the dominant pattern is the long-run downtrend.

support_charts.title: Crude birth rate
support_charts.subtext: Births per 1,000 population across the same history.

support_charts.title: Fertility milestones
support_charts.subtext: Start, latest and historical peak in the total fertility rate.

sections.commentary: The fertility decline is much larger than any temporary rebound, which is why the ageing and household sections reinforce this one.

sections.title: Household downsizing
sections.headline: 2025: 1-2 person households = 56.0% of all households
sections.insight: The one-to-two-person share rose from 31.4% to 56.0% across the series.
sections.chart_note: Annual share computed from Domestic households by household size (excluding foreign domestic helpers).

support_charts.title: One-person households
support_charts.subtext: Share of all domestic households occupied by one person.

support_charts.title: Two-person households
support_charts.subtext: Share of all domestic households occupied by two people.

sections.commentary: Housing demand can keep rising even when headline population slows, because smaller household size increases the number of households that need space.

sources.title: Domestic households by household size (excluding foreign domestic helpers)

sections.title: Household income
sections.headline: 2025: HK$30,000 median monthly income
sections.insight: Median monthly household income rose from HK$13,000 to HK$30,000, a nominal increase of 130.8%.
sections.chart_note: Annual overall median, excluding foreign domestic helpers. This section uses the income level as the main history and the year-on-year rate as a supporting read.

support_charts.title: Income growth rate
support_charts.subtext: Year-on-year change in the annual median household income series.

support_charts.title: Income milestones
support_charts.subtext: Start, latest and peak income levels in nominal HK dollars.

sections.commentary: The long-run rise is clear, but this is a nominal series, so it should be read alongside the inflation section rather than on its own.

sources.title: Median monthly household income by household size (excluding foreign domestic helpers)

sections.title: Labour force participation
sections.headline: 2025: participation 57.0%, labour force 3,811.3 thousand
sections.insight: Participation peaked at 65.1% in 1986 and now sits at 57.0%.
sections.chart_note: Annual averages for both sexes. The participation rate is the cleaner structural signal, while labour force size is kept as a supporting graphic.

support_charts.title: Labour force count
support_charts.subtext: Absolute labour force size in thousands.

support_charts.title: Participation milestones
support_charts.subtext: Start, latest and peak participation readings.

sections.commentary: A large labour-force headcount does not fully offset a softer participation rate, which is why ageing pressure matters for labour supply.

sources.title: Statistics on labour force, employment, unemployment and underemployment

sections.title: Unemployment cycle
sections.headline: 2026-09: 3.9% seasonally adjusted
sections.insight: The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate ranged from 1.0% in 1989-12 to 8.5% in 2003-06.
sections.chart_note: Monthly moving 3-month series from the General Household Survey.

support_charts.title: Recent cycle
support_charts.subtext: A zoomed view of the last 72 monthly observations.

support_charts.title: Shock snapshots
support_charts.subtext: Nearest readings around major event markers plus the latest point.

sections.commentary: Unlike ageing or fertility, unemployment is sharply cyclical. The event markers matter here because labour-market stress tends to cluster around shocks.

sources.title: Statistics on labour force, employment, unemployment and underemployment

sections.title: Real GDP per capita
sections.headline: 2025: HK$440,261 per person in chained dollars
sections.insight: Real GDP per capita climbed from HK$37,449 to HK$440,261. The series high is HK$440,261 in 2025.
sections.chart_note: Annual chained-dollar GDP and real GDP per capita. Event lines are especially useful here because external crises show up clearly in the macro cycle.

support_charts.title: Real GDP level
support_charts.subtext: Chained-dollar GDP level in HK$ million.

support_charts.title: Decade growth
support_charts.subtext: Percentage change versus the previous decade anchor.

sections.commentary: Per-capita output trends upward over the long run, but the distance between event markers and the line makes clear how exposed Hong Kong is to external shocks.

sources.title: Gross Domestic Product (GDP), implicit price deflator of GDP and per capita GDP

sections.title: Inflation regime
sections.headline: 2026-09: 1.9% CPI inflation
sections.insight: Composite CPI inflation ranged from -6.1% in 1999-08 to 16.0% in 1981-10.
sections.chart_note: Monthly year-on-year change in the Composite CPI.

support_charts.title: Recent inflation window
support_charts.subtext: The last 60 monthly observations for a cleaner recent read.

support_charts.title: Event snapshots
support_charts.subtext: Nearest inflation readings around major event markers plus the latest point.

sections.commentary: Inflation in Hong Kong is better read as a sequence of regimes and shocks than as a smooth trend, which is why the event bars add useful context here.
